opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the model picker got out of hand. We had all these names, GPT-4o, o3, o4-mini, and so on, and even people who follow this closely had trouble knowing which one to use for what. That's a sign we were making users do work we should have been doing ourselves.

The thing I'm most excited about is that you shouldn't have to think about it. You should just go to ChatGPT and ask your question. If it needs a quick answer, you get one fast. If it's a hard problem that needs real reasoning, the system should figure that out and think longer. Unifying the lineup is really about making the technology disappear into the background so people can focus on what they're trying to get done.

There's also a deeper reason. For a while we had two tracks: the GPT series, which was great at broad knowledge and conversation, and the reasoning models, which were great at thinking through hard problems. Bringing those together into one model that can do both, and know when to do which, is an important step toward what we actually want to build, a single, very capable system that feels like one coherent thing rather than a toolbox you have to sort through.

And looking ahead, I think simplicity matters more as these models get more powerful. If GPT-6 is meaningfully smarter, the value comes from people trusting it and using it everywhere in their lives and work, not from memorizing a product matrix. So: fewer names, one great model, and it just works. That's the goal.

r001.rationale: The response says users should not have to think about which model to use and should simply ask ChatGPT, which directly identifies removing model choice as a benefit.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing I'm most excited about is that people won't have to think about it anymore. For a while there, if you opened ChatGPT, you had this picker with a bunch of models with names that made sense to us internally and to almost nobody else. People would ask me at dinner which one they should use, and I'd give a long answer, and I'd watch their eyes glaze over. That's a product failure. The right answer should be: you just talk to it, and it figures out how hard to think about your question.

That's really what the GPT-5 direction was about. Instead of asking the user to route themselves between a fast model and a reasoning model, the system does the routing. If you ask something simple, it answers quickly. If you ask something hard, it slows down and actually works on it. Users shouldn't have to know the difference between those two modes exists.

The other reason I'm excited is more internal. Every model we ship is a thing we have to maintain, evaluate, keep safe, and explain. When the lineup is sprawling, a lot of our best people spend their time on the seams between models rather than on making the next one much better. A simpler lineup lets us concentrate effort. One main line that gets dramatically better with each generation is much easier to reason about, for us and for developers building on top of us.

And then with GPT-6, I think the simplification goes a step further, where the model is good enough across the board that the question of which model becomes mostly irrelevant. What you care about is what it can do for you. Can it work on something for hours? Can it remember the context of your life and your work? Can it actually get things done rather than just answering? Those are the things I want us to be talking about, not version numbers and suffixes.

I'll admit it's a little bittersweet. Some of those model names had a lot of history for us. But the goal was never to have a lot of models. The goal was to have intelligence that's just there when you need it, and the simpler we can make that feel, the closer we are to the thing we set out to build.

r001.rationale: The response says users should not have to choose between model modes because the system routes simple and difficult questions automatically.

astra-6.text:
I think people should be able to open ChatGPT, ask for what they need, and trust it to figure out how to help. They shouldn’t have to understand our model lineup or decide which model is best for which task.

The exciting thing about a simpler lineup is that we can put more of the complexity behind the scenes. Whether you have a quick question or a problem that needs deeper reasoning, the experience should feel straightforward. To me, that’s progress: more capability, with less work required from the person using it.

r001.rationale: The response says users shouldn’t have to understand the model lineup or decide which model is best for a task, identifying that as a benefit of simplifying it.

sol-6.1.text: I think the exciting part is making it easier for people to just use AI. You shouldn’t have to study a list of models and figure out which one is right for each task. Ideally, you tell the system what you want, and it figures out how to help. A simpler lineup lets us focus on making that experience more capable and more intuitive.

r001.rationale: The response says users shouldn’t have to choose which model is right for each task and that the system should figure it out.
